Markets & Governance

Huang Steps Down at Nvidia as Bitcoin Breaks $70,000

Four days after backing its founder, Nvidia’s board accepted Jensen Huang’s immediate resignation—rattling tech shares just as $1.3 billion in crypto liquidations, MSCI index deletions, and a $165 million collateral squeeze hit Bitcoin’s price.

Compiled from Nostr dispatches · Markets Desk

On Thursday, NVIDIA Board of Directors announced today that Jensen Huang has resigned as President, Chief Executive Officer, and a member of the Board, effective immediately. [s537] Four days after publicly expressing confidence in its founder, the chipmaker installed chief financial officer Colette Kress as interim chief executive and appointed Harvey Jones as its first board chair [s541, s553]. The announcement followed days of scrutiny over Huang’s personal conduct, U.S. export-control records demanded by Senate Democrats on November 11, and unresolved intelligence allegations involving former Megaspeed executive Alice Huang [s541, s553].

Nvidia shares opened roughly 13 percent lower on Thursday before closing down 4.3 percent at $166.19 [s553, s562]. Commentators across the feed read the ouster in sharply different lights: ManyKeys argued that a founder owning 3.58 percent of shares never held institutional control [s541], Archer Ships contended that backers of closed-model AI rivals stood to gain from removing an open-weight champion [s537], and fiatjaf dryly asked whether Nostr could hire Huang as its chief executive [s242].

Bitcoin fell alongside technology equities and kept sliding overnight, dropping below $72,000 on Thursday morning and breaching $70,000 for the first time since August 19 [s534, s553]. Friday morning dispatches placed spot near $68,622—down nearly 7 percent over 24 hours—with late-window readings dipping to $67,645.05 as more than $1.3 billion in futures positions were liquidated [s2, s534]. Spot exchange-traded funds extended their slide as well, with BlackRock’s IBIT shedding roughly $2 billion across nine straight sessions [s558].

Beneath the spot sell-off sits a mechanical unwind of corporate leverage and index inclusion. MSCI’s November 11 review formally dropped Strategy and Japan’s Metaplanet from its flagship benchmarks effective after the November 30 close, forcing passive tracking funds to sell roughly 13 million Strategy shares even though neither company is required to sell coins [s529, s553].

More acute pressure surfaced in Nashville, where Bitcoin treasury firm Nakamoto Inc. disclosed in an SEC 8-K that it owes exchange Kraken 165 million USDT against a roughly $104 million market capitalization, with 3,030 of its 4,283 bitcoin pledged as collateral at an average purchase cost of $118,171 [s550, s562]. A November 11 loan amendment pushed a $60 million tranche from December 2026 to December 2027, leaving $105 million due June 30, 2027 [s550].

Hard money does not protect anyone from their own leverage. It only makes the bill arrive in the currency that cannot be printed, on a date that was agreed in advance, and it does not negotiate.

From The Collateral Chain by Roger [s562].

Elsewhere in corporate treasuries, Rumble disclosed it sold roughly two-thirds of its bitcoin stack during the third quarter as its Quake AI cloud division delivered its first adjusted profit [s556], while JPMorgan’s Q3 13F showed a 36 percent increase in Strategy shares and BNY Mellon raised its stake in Strive by 28 percent as of September 30 [s554, s557]. With U.S. 10-year Treasury yields above 5.1 percent and traders pricing in a December Federal Reserve rate hike, analysts noted that capital-cost gravity is repricing proxies faster than the underlying protocol [s534, s562].

Protocol & Sovereignty

Browsers, Signers, and the Economics of Free Software
Software & Architecture

Nostr Browsers, Sovereign Vaults, and a Governance Debate

Builders shipped standalone identity signers, Ark server directories, and a Nostr-native browser—even as skeptics argued the protocol lacks corporate capital.

A wave of infrastructure releases arrived across the feed over the past 24 hours. Cody released PsstPsst v26.11.1, adding support for napps, napplets, nsites, and conventional websites in a bid to turn the client into a Nostr browser [s74]. FBO Developments Sàrl graduated its identity vault and NIP-46/NIP-55 signer CustID out of beta to version 1.0.0, keeping keys in hardware-backed Android storage with no Google Play Services [s542, s605].

Elsewhere, Christoph Ono launched a directory for (B)Ark servers at servers.arke.cash [s33], Zapstore 2.0 drew praise from René Aaron and franzap [s30, s141], and fiatjaf pointed users to a Verdana client bootstrap at pyramid.fiatjaf.com/verdana [s122].

Not everyone agreed on Nostr’s trajectory. User zk argued that current gatekeepers are disconnected from mainstream adoption and that attracting real business capital requires adding a corporate governance layer into the NIPs [s14].

Highlights & Custody

Why Freedom Tech Resists Ownership—and Why Custody Keeps Drifting

Two highlighted passages captured the tension between uncapturable protocols and paying customers, just as LNMarkets announced KYC and Fedi urged users to migrate.

Readers surfaced sharp passages from the essay Freedom doesn’t pay. As its author wrote in an excerpt marked by Azz: the reality is: freedom tech simply can’t be sold. It’s the wrong shape. Freedom tech resists ownership; who is going to buy something that is designed to not be controlled? [s523]

In another excerpt from the same essay highlighted by Nate, the author reflected on trying to commercialize protocol work: Every effort I’ve made to bend Nostr to my potential customers’ will has resulted in compromise on the vision that got me into the space. [s526] Commenting on the essay, Alex Gleason argued that open relay broadcasting invites the same spam and cruelty as legacy platforms, contending that Nostr works best inside smaller, trusted author circles [s525].

Meanwhile, custody boundaries tightened elsewhere. Flix noted that Lightning derivatives platform LNMarkets announced it will introduce identity verification in early 2027, quoting its notice: To keep building, LN Markets is becoming a regulated platform, so account verification is coming in early 2027. [s286] Fedi issued a second reminder for federation members to move funds ahead of upgrades [s39], while Mostro asked users to open channels to its relocated Lightning node [s1].

Security & Research

Quantum Timelines, Wallet Implants, and Probing Math

IBM’s 520-qubit processor misses the depth required to break secp256k1, while hardware-implant reports and two self-hosting vulnerabilities call for prompt patching.

IBM’s unveiling of its 520-qubit Nighthawk r3 processor at the Quantum Developer Conference prompted fresh headlines, but an analysis by 21 Milioni di Chiacchiere noted that IBM is scaling qubit width rather than error-corrected circuit depth [s540]. Breaking 256-bit elliptic curves requires thousands of logical qubits and billions of Toffoli gates—thresholds IBM’s own roadmap places beyond 2033 with Blue Jay, well after Starling’s 200-logical-qubit milestone in 2029 [s540]. Still, analysts noted roughly 6.9 million BTC already sit in addresses with exposed public keys, giving weight to draft post-quantum proposals like bc1z and basic address hygiene [s534, s540, s562].

Closer to present threats, Trezor disclosed unauthorized hardware implants intercepted in three Safe 5 wallets sold by a former Southeast Asian reseller, designed to exfiltrate displayed seed phrases over cellular networks; firmware 2.13.1 blocks the implant from reading screens [s534]. Trezor Suite 26.11.1 also added warnings before sending to never-before-used addresses [s539].

Freedom.Tech’s daily brief flagged urgent patches for exposed self-hosters: Uptime Kuma 2.5.11 (admin-only remote code execution) and Radicale 3.9.1 (an empty-credential auth bypass), alongside routine updates to Tails 7.17, Session Desktop 1.18.4, StartOS 0.4.2, and Nostr relay Citrine 3.2.4, which stopped storing contact lists for unfollowed strangers [s539].

In Lightning research, Amboss published a peer-reviewed Algorithms paper showing Bayesian Binary Search speeds up channel balance probing by 3 to 6 percent in production [s345]. Meanwhile, ARK Research calculated that crypto hackers have stolen $26.9 billion since 2017—57 cents for every dollar of onchain revenue—with 2026 losses of $8.7 billion already outpacing full-year revenue projections [s549].

World & Craft

Dispatches Across Borders, Housing, and the Feed
Financial Freedom Report

Currency Controls, Exchange Exits, and Restored Reserves

From Beirut’s frozen-dollar settlements to New York’s ban on surveillance pricing, financial sovereignty remained contested on every front.

In Lebanon, seven years after banks froze dollar accounts, large depositors are being offered settlements in real estate, bonds, or bank shares at 15,000 pounds per dollar—a steep haircut against parallel market rates [s60, s527]. In Russia, exchanges KuCoin, Bitget, and MEXC exited the market in October as the Kremlin advances its digital ruble, while in Egypt a court ordered independent outlet Mada Masr closed and fined editor Lina Attalah 3 million Egyptian pounds [s527].

Regulators pressed elsewhere too: India’s public-sector Indian Overseas Bank launched a programmable digital rupee app [s527], the IMF urged Kenya to link names, addresses, and IDs across crypto transfers [s85], and Paraguay’s central bank chief warned over biometric databases left behind by collapsed ueno bank [s96]. Meanwhile, evacide celebrated the New York City Council passing a ban on personal-data surveillance pricing [s16].

On settlement rails, the Liquid Network restored full 1:1 bitcoin backing following September’s $320 million exploit [s527], Binance reported covering its $6.34 billion October 29 breach with company funds while reopening withdrawals in phases [s560], and Israel Discount Bank prepared a closed-wallet bitcoin trading launch for November 26 [s559].

Macro, Energy & Policy

U.S. Home Sales Sink to 16-Year Low as AI Competes for Stranded Power

Mortgage rates above 7.3 percent froze October transactions, while institutional capital backed modular inference containers and German bitcoiners debated tax relief.

October U.S. existing home sales dropped 5.5 percent to a 3.75 million seasonally adjusted annual rate, the lowest reading since August 2010, as 30-year mortgage rates averaged 7.33 percent [s552]. Median prices still crept up 0.4 percent year-over-year to $416,700—the 40th straight monthly gain—even as first-time buyers fell to 29 percent of purchases [s552].

Home buying is difficult when mortgage rates have climbed to their highest levels since 2000, aside from a single month in 2023. As a result, home sales fell to their lowest level since August 2010. [s552] National Association of Realtors chief economist Lawrence Yun’s assessment underscored a market locked by illiquidity rather than active buyer competition [s552].

In energy infrastructure, Salt Lake City startup Torus closed a $500 million Series C led by Magnetar to mass-produce Foundry, prefabricated 1-to-20 MW AI inference units that install behind existing transformers in 12 to 16 weeks—bypassing multi-year grid queues with the stranded-power playbook Bitcoin miners pioneered [s551]. Meanwhile, markusturm reported that Germany’s Bitcoin community met a tabloid claim that the one-year tax-free holding period would survive with skepticism after Bundestag lawmaker Frank Schäffler warned it was only a postponement [s533].

People & Craft

Forged Keys, Olive Harvests, and Ordinary Thursdays

Between sourdough telemetry and Sicilian olive groves, the human half of the feed kept its own slower clock.

Away from price charts, builders and growers posted notes from workbenches and orchards. Modulo shared metalwork for durable backups—Liquid starlight from the universe’s furnaces melted, refined, rolled, and cut for you to make your unique bitcoin key. [s221] In Sicily, SatsOil compared mining blocks to harvesting olives under low time preference [s187].

Baker and hardware tinkerer pam detailed months of sourdough loaves alongside a $6 ESP32 and infrared-sensor starter monitor that pings Telegram when dough doubles [s4]. Timothy Allen interviewed Stacia Wilson about Meridia, a planned federated town near Austin [s42], while danielw posted a 2022 photograph of Christchurch’s Dandelion Fountain [s79] and APOD highlighted stellar nursery NGC 206 in Andromeda [s119].

The day’s quietest note came from Jody Baer on the one-year anniversary of finding her late father: Despite being the worst day of my life, life somehow continued on. And now, here we are. Just a normal Thursday. [s127]
